chapters.label: Chapter 1
chapters.title: One Bad Story
paras: Watching her die was satisfying. But there is something about taking human life that makes you want to cry. Whichever way you looked at it, the maxim was accurate: There is no justice, only revenge. All killers are unjustified in their reasons or lack thereof. Staring down the body of my first kill, I came to understand that killing was a trait born of sheer arrogance. People killed because a part of them felt they were better than their victims. Of course, I, too, had my reasons, unjustifiable as they may be.
I wasn't arrogant, but I’d had enough.

As usual, our family's problems begin with Merceides. He is impulsive and never stays put. He is never careful; he goes out at the most inopportune times, into dangerous places, recklessly, and barely ever listens to advice. I’m going to narrate this part of the story the way the others told it to me. You must forgive me; I am not big on storytelling.
It was 7:46 p.m., the bar was as scanty as a bald man’s head, and the situation was, in the simplest of terms, awkward.
"Shouldn't we order something?" Jane said, trying her best to lighten our moods.
"We could," Hadeezah replied. Her eyes were a saw cutting through my body.
"Well, I'll be right back," Jane said and zoomed away like a guilty bee leaving us staring at each other, stung.
Hadeezah, who had wanted to stop her, was now stuck with me. It didn't seem to be the best option.
"I don't know who that woman is."
"It doesn't matter."
"She said she came to pay me back a part of the outrageous fee her husband— Ex-husband took from me."
"And she put it in your mouth?"
She slammed the menu on the edge of the table in a slap so loud that Jane and a few others turned around to look.
"They're working something out," Jane told Danny.
"I was as surprised as you are."
She looked at my face for a moment before letting the menu fall lightly onto the table.
"I guess I expected differently."
"As you should. I am not in the habit of receiving payments through my mouth. It's cuckoo. I'm not a pigeon."
She giggled. It sounded like the coy sound of a happy baby.
"So, what's your favourite on the menu?" I asked, now that she seemed a bit more relaxed.
"I've never had anything here," she said. "I've only ever come once."
"You don't seem to be the type to go out a lot."
"I do want to go out, but I don't think it will be an experience I'll enjoy."
"Why? Our youthful debauchery too crude for you?"
She laughed again. "It's all right to do that—to drink, get high, smoke, and use drugs. But it doesn't last."
This time I laughed.
"What's funny?"
"You don't look the type to chase after a high, that's all." "Is there a type when it comes to living?"
"Well—"
"Sorry to interrupt you two lovebirds, but you've got to order something. My establishment don't fuel itself on romance."
"We're not—" Hadeezah started.
"We'll have whatever's best on the menu. Probably a serving from the top ten."
"You mean that, buddy?" Danny's eyes widened. His prickly grey beard spread into a hairy grin.
"You accept crypto?"
"Damn, I'd take anything,” he said and yelled, "Service!"
A fidgeting waitress came over. She seemed stressed and nervous. I would have felt sorry for her had Danny not turned on the news.
She received her orders, and Danny left us, remote in hand, pointing at the TV and raising the volume.

"Our very own Merceides, a member of the Senate, has been caught on video fleeing the scene of a crime and is wanted by police for an investigation into several other killings and a murder in Abu Dis."
"Merceides is living the life." Hadeezah smiled.
"That's some way to live," I said, my mind racing on what Merceides might have gotten himself into this time. Jane seemed to be occupied talking to some guy in a suit.
"Would you like to get out of here?"
"But we just ordered." She protested.

I waved the waitress over and made a transfer, paying for everything and requesting two packs of their best. Gladly, she breezed into the kitchen and was back with two nylon packs. I took them both and handed her a generous tip.
"Shall we?"
She took my hand. She was soft, like memory foam. We sneaked out into the dark, leaving Jane engrossed in her conversation.
"You're not a serial killer, are you?" Hadeezah asked when the night air was wheezing by as we walked through the trees into nowhere in particular.
"And you waited all this time to ask me. Are you?"
"Haha—. I might be. What would you do if I were one?"
"Probably tell you to take your time, take it slow."
She appeared flushed.
"I mean, with the killing. "Take it slow" means you should slit my veins and let me die so we both get what we want. You get a death, and I get to watch you a while longer while I die."
"Oh— Oh! Oh!—"
"By that response, I gather you are not a serial killer?"
"God no! I couldn't bear it on my conscience. So, you've skilfully failed to answer if you are one."
"We're all killers. How often we kill is the difference."
We had walked into a clearing with a boulder. Above, the sky was lit with a splash of starry gems. We sat on the rock and dropped the food packs between us.
"The stars are beautiful tonight." She said, looking heavenward.
I stared at her and quickly turned my eyes away. She reminded me of the night I had spent with Nadia staring at the stars. If only that night had not ended.
"So, what did they give us?" She took off her Jean jacket and laid it beside her.

I opened a pack and peered into it. “Lettuce and fish, with iodine sprinkled on it. It smells like ketchup, but I doubt its integrity. You’re sure Danny sells NAFDAC-approved foods? Because I don’t think goat lung prepared by that Junior WAEC style chef and a touch of dysentery are my preferred choice of foods.”
By now, she was laughing so hard that I feared her back would snap in two the way she was bent backwards, both hands on the rock, as she laughed into the sky.
“Perhaps we should turn our attention from Danny’s place to you.”
“Me?” I closed the pack and dropped it into the bag. “I know how to fry an egg.”
She laughed in continuity. “That’s not what I meant,” she said after catching her breath.
“What did you mean, Hadeezah?” I shifted the bag to my back and moved closer to her. She appeared to be cold because she seemed to freeze.
“Cain—”

I edged closer. Strangely, it did not feel strange or unnatural for me to want her. She felt like something I’ve always had, like she was mine and I’d only been away. It was like leaving your food on the table to get the TV remote. You come back to it without caution because you have its taste in your mouth, and I was looking at her lips.
I raised my hand to her face and stroked away a lock of hair. Her breath grazed my skin, anxious and hot. I could tell from it how fast her heart was racing.
“Cain—” She sighed as my hand touched lightly on her face.

She was close, and she was all that was present in the universe for me. I placed my hand on hers on the rock as we drew closer to each other. Her pupils were dilated, and her breath was coming in short, fast bursts. I could feel tremors run through her body and into mine. I could smell her hair, her sweat, and the chemicals that ran underneath her skin’s pores. It was as if I were intoxicated.
Our lips were about to meet when a blow hit my stomach so hard it sent me rolling off the rock onto the ground.

For a moment, I was thrown into oblivion. However, the pain brought a wave of searing anger to my chest when I opened my eyes and saw a man trying to pull her away while another, the one who hit me, stormed closer. All the rage I'd felt in the past seemed to coalesce into one dark goal: to kill them both.

I lay on the ground as the man with Hadeezah tried to put her over his shoulder while the other approached me menacingly. I clutched on to a piece of rock, closed my eyes, and waited. When he came, I groaned and placed my hand on my stomach. The other man was still struggling with her, with his back turned to us.
This man, who was almost twice my size, towered over me and laughed. It seemed this wasn’t his first rodeo.
“Please, leave her alone.” I sighed, clutching the rock harder. One mistake, and this bazooka could blow my ribs straight off.
“We’ll take good care of her.” He laughed. “It’s you who should be concerned, pretty boy.”
As he raised his leg to smash his boot into me, I rolled over and hurled my body into the air like an NBA player, smashing the rock on the front of his head.
Without waiting to see if he was down, I ran to the other man, who was unprepared. Turning to see who was approaching, he was met by a blow so hard I forgot my fist in his face.
“You scoundrel.” I heard a voice behind me say.

Unfortunately, the other man was up. If Hadeezah were some other girl, I would have told her to run. But I knew better. Before I could think about it, she picked up a rock and threw it in the man’s direction. Unluckily for both of us, she missed. I was thinking about the unheroic course of action when the man who was down caught her by the leg. She screamed and started to kick at him. In that moment of distraction, the other man gripped me by the shoulder and was about to return my fist, which I would have hated— a lot.

I gritted my teeth and was waiting to duck in reflex when a side jab to the stomach from his back sent him to his knees. My knowledge of anatomy told me the blow had hit his kidney. With his grip released, I let my hand fly in a full blow that met his windpipe. He crashed to the ground, choking.
My saviour and I then turned our attention to the other man, who was getting to his knees. Seeing the board balanced, he got to his feet and fled, the other man wheezing right after him.
“Are you alright?” Kane asked, approaching Hadeezah.
“Yes, thank you!”
I observed that she seemed to recoil from him.
“Thank you, Kane,” I said.
No sooner was I done than he sprang on me, landing us both on the ground. Whatever kind of night this was, I sure wasn’t prepared for it.
“Kane!” Multiple voices yelled.
I could see Harvey and Jane materialising in our little scene. Great!
“You never put her in harm’s way, you understand?”
“I understand. Now, could you get off me? You’re not my type.”
He smiled.
The others came to gather around us as he pulled me up.
“Stop bullying people,” Hadeezah said, poking Kane with a finger. I imagined a kid poking a lion with a stick and smiled. He smiled too and stared her down.
“We’re okay,” I said and went toward her.
“Any idea what they wanted?” Kane asked.
“I was too busy to ask. But I could send a fax tomorrow.”
There was dead silence until Harvey laughed. “I think I like this guy,” he said.
“You two best be coming along with us,” Jane said, grabbing the bag we’d left on the rock.

Afar off in the shadows, a man watched the whole scene with silent contentment. He thought, stroked his beard, and drove off to the other end of the road, where he waited in his tinted glass car until the two beat-up men emerged, dragging their self-esteem with them. They stopped near the door as the man extended a handful of cash.
“And some extra for expenses,” he said.
“Thank you.” They nodded in appreciation.
“I didn’t know he was so strong,” the bigger man said.
“Nor did I,” the man in the car replied as he rolled up his tints and drove away.

chapters.label: Chapter 2
chapters.title: How They Were
paras: You must understand that this part of the story is a narration of events I pieced together myself. Kane is not much of a talker and he never told me much of what transpired between he and Hadeezah. Jane, too, isn’t much of a reliable witness given her propensity to exaggerate. I would have confirmed my inferences from Harvey, but I decided it best to keep to myself. So, you’d have to settle for my story.
I think, t’was the night before Christmas, and as meat was not an uncommon diet during this season.

Kane killed the man, butchered, the body, and placed the parts in a bag alongside the cows. He left the door open and dragged the bag to the mill, with the intent to grind the bones into bird feed. He took one last look at the dismembered body before tossing it into the grinder. He would be dried, sold out, and eaten before anyone would know he was missing. It was what he deserved. If a man's life was shit, his death deserved no respect.

He watched as all evidence disappeared, then he went back up and proceeded to wash the blood off the floor. He looked up and saw her curtain fall from the side. She had been watching him again. He didn't mind. He finished and glanced up again to see her watching from parted curtains. He deduced that her family was wealthy. But she'd lost both parents. He wondered what her room smelled like. She probably slept looking up at flowers on the ceiling. It reminded him of housekeeping.
Mrs Hess came out of her house. More like proceeded. She needed a change of lifestyle or a bigger door frame.
"Season's greeting." He yelled!
His voice startled her. When she came to, she nodded and hurried back into the house, almost trapping herself at the door.

He laughed. When he looked up, he saw her smiling. She caught him looking at her, and she waved. He stared, and then, went back into the house and shut the door with a bang that jittered the area code's nerves.

If only he could see her. She was about to turn from the curtain when Mrs Frederick escaped from her house. She watched with amusement as the woman sniffed her way to the corner of the house and whistled for her dogs.

The Danes were always at Kane's place. He took his time to prepare meals for them. And it was a lot more than he gave her, in terms of attention. He understood animals. Maybe that was why he loved to kill them.
She wondered what he was like as a person.

Mrs Frederick whistled, and the dogs bounded out of his garden. As she bent to attend to them, Kane came out with two bowls of blood meal. The dogs ran to greet him, leaving her bent halfway. She gave him a grave look, which he returned with a dead stare.
The girl at the window chuckled.

In a just world, Mrs Frederick would have been complete with whiskers and a tail. She schlepped nervously back to her door and waited for the dogs to finish eating before whistling them over again. He nodded to her and kept his usual look. A grim countenance that could scare the black out of a raven.
"Merry Christmas, Kane."
He nodded and turned his attention away. Mrs Frederick was an optimistic sanguine who placed courtesy before fear, frequently using one to cover up the constant emergence of the other.
She used her legs to shoo the dogs in and with reverence, shut her door. As if she feared the sound might upset him.

They were alone again, and the streets were silent. He looked up at her window and peered for a while. She stared at him, holding her breath, afraid that he might stop looking. And then after forever passed, she waved. He stared, more intently this time, and then, taking his hand from his pocket, he looked at his watch and went back into the house as if she never existed. And it hurt.

The rays of the evening sun splashed on the roofs like orange juice, as Kane busied himself thinking through past events. In the eventuality that Mr Norman was declared missing, he would not want it to be traced back to him.
He moved closer to his window, avoiding the light, to observe the street more clearly.

Two men were engaged in a heated conversation as they walked by. Mr Thompson, the postman and Mr Douglas the shoemaker. It was a pity; Santa would be AWOL this year. He smiled. The thought of what might happen if anyone knew what he had done was intriguing. He didn't feel fear, just scientific fascination concerning that night.

He shifted his attention to the house opposite his. Her curtains were cream and thin, almost see-through. At night, he could make out her silhouette as she walked around the room, sometimes in a robe, sometimes not.

Kane was a realist. A quality sharply contrasted to his handsome features. Chiselled where he should be, with black eyes and a straight nose, he could pass for altruistic, if not for the depth of his gaze. A piercing look that gave clarity to an unspoken mantra: his Impatience.
He was still watching when her front door opened. It was Jane. They laughed, and Jane went her way. The girl stayed a while outside, sipping in the orange sunlight.
She could not look misfit in whatever clothes she wore. The Jean wore her body like her skin was denim. He swallowed.
She was about to go in when Tyrone, the pharmacist, caught up to her. He appeared to be on his way home from work or stalking her.
Kane clenched his fists.
Tyrone gave her something in a little bag. She took one out and tore the wrapper open.

Chocolate again! Kane scoffed. He watched her wave Tyrone away, leaving the simpleton with rosy cheeks. Suddenly, she crossed over to the front of his house, dropped a chocolate bar on the doorstep and went back into her house, leaving him alone, neglected.
It was past midnight when Kane slipped out from the back of the house. He instinctively smelt the chocolate bar after picking it up.

Nighttime sharpened his instincts. The will to survive was spurred on by superstitious fear and the knowledge that the owners of the night were more ferocious predators than men. He tore the wrapper open and snapped the chocolate in two, melting it in his mouth.
Her lights were out, and the whole neighbourhood was asleep. It was 3:00 a.m. in northern Nigeria.

He sat on the third step and observed the stars. There was something about the sky that made man want to go beyond the earth. To him, it was proof that a God did exist. Beyond them was uninhabited territory in total space. But it was not the space that called. It was the voice of the night that spoke to him.

In a few hours, it would be daylight, and everyone would be wishing each other a Merry Christmas, until they realised that, unlike previous years, Mr Norman, the philanthropist, Santa, had not appeared.

He wondered how God would judge his act. Would it be based on intent, the cruelty of his deed, or the satisfaction he derived from its execution? But God was a killer too, was He not? After all, they both killed with reason whoever had unjustly wronged others.
Kane was ready to pay for his crime, were he ever caught. He had a few more names to erase. When he was done, he would find another purpose or peace. But for now, vengeance was all he had.

He went to the garden and rummaged in the dearth of flowers and vines. He pulled up a rose, and finding a tin can, poured some water into it. Dissatisfied, he pulled up another rose and wrapped them both with a vine before placing them into a clean water filled bottle.

Crossing the street, he folded the chocolate wrapper neatly and placed it under the bottle. Leaving them beside the door of her house. Then like the night, he disappeared into his house to hibernate, before the chaos that would unfold by Christmas eve.

He watched her from behind the curtains. She had been surprised to see the roses. She had smiled when she saw the chocolate wrapper underneath. Odd way to send a Christmas card, she must have thought.
She was still examining it when Jane called to her.

Jane was funny in a three-legged cat kind of way. She hopped down the steps like a hare. Almost losing her balance, she clung to the girl, spilling some water from the bottle. They went in, with Jane yapping about something.

He left the window and went downstairs to the back of his house. The house was large with a basement underneath, a garage on the left and a garden on the right that spread to the back. He spent most of his time in the garden, plotting.

The apple tree there was at least ten years old. He loved the birds that lived on it. They were not around at afternoons. They, like men, had gone to work. They liked him though. He fed them; still, they went far to gather food. But they always came back.

He plucked an apple and was about to sink his teeth into it when he sensed a new scent. He turned to see the girls crossing the street to the garden. Jane had excitement written all over. He watched them approach. Jane carefree, the other cautious, but not hesitant.
"Merry Christmas, Kane!" She yelled, as if she were not close enough.
"Fucking nuisance." He murmured, as he approached the fence.
He faced them squarely, with a straight and disinterested gaze.
"Merry Christmas, Jane," he said. He gazed at the other girl and caught her eye. Almost habitually, she raised her hand slightly and waved.
"HI!" She said, in words that she almost swallowed.

His piercing gaze was now focused on her. A look so loud, even Jane fell uncomfortably silent. For a moment, it seemed like the world should crash so she would disappear, but then he raised his hand a little above his waist and waved back.
"Hi!"

Things might not exactly add up, but you get the picture of Eutopia I’m trying to paint. Kane lived in isolation with Harvey as his bridge to humanity. The girls lived together, and the neighbours left Kane alone. It was the ideal neighbourhood and no one was the wiser of anyone else’s activities.

chapters.label: Chapter 3
chapters.title: The Original Santa
paras: From what I gather, it was raining when the van stopped in front of the house. The men got down; their hands tucked into their raincoats. The one in front was big and hairy, like a human furball.

They knocked twice. The first with their hands, the second with the butt of a gun. Kane was in his usual hiding place when his father opened the door. It was hide-and-seek Monday, and father was pretending not to know where he was.

When the door opened, they walked in without invitation, and Kane froze. There were four men, all of them built like bears, but it was the fifth man that made him freeze. Kane could sense intentions, and this man, he was sure, was not pure in heart.
They forced his father to sit, and when his little brother came yelling excitedly, his father wanted to shoo him away, but the bad man picked him up, tucking him between his legs.

The ceiling was getting hotter, but Kane could not move. The men were trying to force his father into signing a paper, but his father refused until the bad man pulled out a gun and placed it close to his brother's head. Kane couldn't breathe, but there was nothing he could do.
He watched as his father signed the paper, and then begged the men to leave.
"Thank you." The man said, in a voice so soft it felt friendly. "Where is the other boy?"
"He went for a sleepover."

The man smiled and nodded to the other men, who took his father by the shoulders and took his brother from him. He told them to let the little rascal be. So they let his brother run, and just when he got to the kitchen door, the hiss of the bullet sounded, cutting his life short at the age of four.
The man laughed. A horrible sound that would haunt Kane for life. He left the house and drove away, leaving the men to beat his father to death.
Kane watched everything, absorbing every blow, every broken bone and snap, every crack. When they were done, they stabbed his father's heart and let him bleed away on the floor. Kane watched him die.

Kane waited until their car drove away, then he waited until nightfall, then until he could move. When he came down, he didn't cry; he just stared at the bodies and then went to his father's vault, packed everything up into a bag like his father had taught him to and left the house, after sprinkling a bag of -O blood from the stairs to the door.

Kane took his time. He went through the list every day, crossing out names until he had found all five men. There was a sixth, an unnamed man. All that he found in the files was half a face from a torn picture he had taken with the others in a group.

He had grown up alone, but unlike what his father always said, he never changed his name. A name was an identity, but it was all he had left. He had found his way to the countryside, wandering until he'd found a piece of land. He'd purchased it under his false name. He made sure the houses he purchased always had a basement. They were vital to his escape.

He spent the first year observing the farmers and locking himself indoors. Whoever asked, he told that he was waiting for his parents. In the second year, he hired help. He was 12 now and had decided that the affairs of his father's death were long forgotten. It was time to act.

Harvey, whom he hired, was to serve as his legal guardian, swearing an oath on his life to keep all his secrets. He found that he trusted Harvey. The man, 27, had a nonchalance about him that Kane admired.

When he was 13, Kane left the farm for America, where he joined the army. With his knowledge of strategy, a gift he had acquired from his father, he was able to convince the commander to allow him to prove himself. He was allowed into the field at 15, where he fought his way up to special ops. Then at 21, he became a Navy SEAL and at 22, left the army with all the high hopes his commander had for him.

He returned to South Africa that year and went to live on the farm. But things had changed. Most of the old neighbours were dead, and those who remained still remembered him as a sulky little boy who paid attention to no one.

Harvey was happy to have him back. Kane was grateful for the man's assistance. During his leave, the man had demolished the house and turned it from a shabby farmhouse into a stone mansion, the only one in the whole brick neighbourhood.

Kane had used the army as cover for his mission. During his stay, he found those four men and killed them all. He beat them to death, breaking their bones like they did his father. When he returned home, there was only the fifth man left. He had not identified the sixth, but he would.

Kane, who had opened an abattoir near his house on the estate, drove away to the city on the 20th of December to drop Harvey off at his family's home and create his alibi. Harvey did not ask questions; he understood.

At 11:47 p.m., Kane left the house on foot and jogged into the busy town with fireworks and a rifle in his bag. In the crowd that was as happy as the season allowed, he got lost until he emerged on a roof, quiet and unaffected by the jubilation of the public.

He had paid some kids to play a prank. At 12:59, they were to start lighting up the fireworks in front of the rich man's house. They gladly accepted the offer because the rich man used his dogs and guards to scare them away.

He assembled the rifle and waited; it was 12:50. He recalled his brother as he lay dying on the floor, close to the kitchen door. He had been shot at exactly 1:00 that day. He waited, and then he heard the first bang. It was 12:59.

When the lights came on, the children rose from their beds, and Mr Norman drudged downstairs in his pyjamas. Kane waited until the light came on in the room of Mr Norman's son. It was his youngest child, his only son.

He waited for the boy to open the bedroom door and start walking down the stairs. The fireworks were still going off, and the guards were trying to scare the kids off. But they could not touch the fireworks since they were all lit up and going off all around the house.

Mr Norman came outside and started yelling orders to the men at the gate. Kane waited and watched the boy. He was about 16, but he had observed him. He was spoilt and as cruel as his father. He waited until the boy reached the kitchen and then, when the fireworks went off, he took the shot.

No one heard the glass crack. Mr Norman was still busy yelling at the men, and there were about 6 more fireworks about to go off. The bullet pierced through the boy's head, splattering blood and brains all over the kitchen.
Kane smiled as he pieced the rifle apart. He climbed down the stairs and left the premises, jogging back with the bag, lighter than he had come.

He observed the funeral. Mr Norman was distraught but tried his best to keep things normal. The burial arrangements had been made in haste. Mr Norman seemed to want to have the business done before Christmas. He had tightened security around the house and secured the fences with electric cables. But that was not where Kane would get him.

After the funeral, he approached Mr Norman, who was drowning in a crowd of sympathisers. He swallowed his disdain and converted it to sadness so it could sit well on his face. He was the last in the queue. Mr Norman seemed eager to leave.

He edged closer and stood in the man's way. Kane was not muscular. He looked like a casual athlete who could jump through hoops in the field and in real-life problems. But there was something in his eyes that froze people. The guard came closer. Normally, he would have laid hands on him, but the man stared him down.
"What is it you want?" Mr Norman said. The others around stared at them, and silence filled the hall.
"It's about your son," he said. Then he bent closer to whisper into the man's ears, hands in his pockets. "He was involved in a drug deal gone bad, sir."
Mr Norman regained his composure, seemingly undisturbed by the information. He was the boy's father, and he had covered his tracks for him.
"Shall we talk outside?" The man said.
Kane nodded.

They went out into the open after he had waved the guards away. Mr Norman liked chewing gum. He pulled out a pack from his coat and started to chew. Kane watched the vein at the side of his head and retained his cool.
"How much does he owe you?" Mr Norman suddenly asked.
"Nothing, sir, but perhaps you can,” Mr Norman looked up at him, waiting for the rest.
"I heard that you like delivering punishments yourself. Perhaps, you can owe me when I get you your son's killer."
Mr Norman stared at him for a while and then produced a cross from around his neck. He held it close as he replied.
"I have found salvation; I will not go down the path of the unrighteous."

Kane pulled out a card and handed it to the man. "That is the address of the hotel I am at." He paused as the man examined the card: "Many people have killed in the name of God. Others have died for less. But a father wanting vengeance for his son, even God will understand. Is that not why the devil suffers so?"
So saying, he made the sign of the cross and left. Leaving Mr Norman a chance at redemption.

Kane knew he was being watched. So he made sure not to make any calls. It wasn't until midnight that they made their move. He had turned the lights off, pretending to be asleep. And then he had rolled off the bed and crawled to the chair hidden in the shadows covered by the wall.

He perched on the chair as the door opened. Two men walked in and stood at opposite sides of the bed, and then a third followed. As if rehearsed, they grabbed the body that was supposedly under the sheets only to discover that it was all pillows.
"I would seriously consider my next move, sir,” Kane cut their surprise short by breathing air behind Mr Norman's neck.
"Leave,” Mr Norman said.
When they were alone, Kane retreated to the dark, where he felt comfortable.
"$2 million,” Mr Norman said. "I want him alive."
"$2 million it is." He knew enough to know that Mr Norman did not negotiate. "23rd December."
"Send me the location; I'll be alone. I will pay a million now, the other when it's done."
"$2 million in Ether, when it is complete."
Mr Norman nodded and stood up. "I trust this will remain between us?"
"It will if you stop. I know you've been searching for me."
"23rd,” Mr Norman said as he left and closed the door.

Kane sat in the shadows, gun in hand. He felt nothing. His place in hell was reserved, but he wouldn't go there with half-served justice on his mind. The thought gave him satisfaction: that his enemy would pay him $2 million to take his life.
He smiled. A rich man's death; others usually died for free.
